opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was honestly one of the more surprising things to watch. The intuition going in was that if you wanted a model to do well on something like GPQA, which is graduate-level physics, chemistry, and biology questions, you'd need to train heavily on those specific domains. And instead we were seeing that training on math, where you have really clean, verifiable answers, was carrying over to science questions the model hadn't been specifically trained on.

My read is that what's transferring isn't the content so much as the *way of thinking*. Math forces the model to break a problem into steps, keep track of what it knows versus what it's assuming, check its work, and back up when something doesn't add up. A lot of hard science questions reward exactly that same discipline. Often the domain facts are necessary but not sufficient, and the hard part is carrying a chain of reasoning through without making a careless leap.

It also made me a bit more humble about benchmarks. When you see a jump on GPQA, it's tempting to say the model "learned more chemistry," but it might really be getting better at reasoning carefully under uncertainty. That's part of why I care so much about building evals that look like real work, because you want to know what capability is actually driving the number, not just that the number went up.

And I think it was an early hint of something bigger: general reasoning ability generalizes. That's exciting, because it means improvements in one area can lift a lot of others at once.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, that was one of the moments that made me sit up a little. We'd been doing reinforcement learning on math problems, and the thing you'd naively expect is that the model gets better at math. Maybe a bit of spillover into adjacent stuff like competition-style logic puzzles. What you don't necessarily expect is that it starts doing noticeably better on GPQA, which is graduate-level physics, chemistry, and biology questions written by domain experts to be hard to Google.

And the key thing is that nothing in the training data looked like those questions. There were no biology questions in the mix. So what was transferring? The best interpretation I have is that what the model was really learning wasn't math facts, it was how to think. How to break a problem down, hold a chain of reasoning in its head, check its own work, notice when a step doesn't follow, back up and try something else. Math is just a very clean, very verifiable domain for practicing those skills, because you get a crisp signal about whether you were right. And it turns out those habits are pretty domain-general. A hard organic chemistry question rewards the same kind of careful, step-by-step, "wait, does that actually hold" reasoning.

I'd caveat it a bit. The gains weren't uniform, and some of the GPQA improvement could be the model simply getting better at reading a dense, multi-part question and not losing track of the constraints, which is a sort of mundane but real skill. And GPQA is a benchmark, which means it's a proxy. Doing well on it doesn't mean the model can run a lab or make a novel scientific contribution.

But as a signal, I found it genuinely encouraging, because it suggested the thing we were training was closer to general reasoning capability than to narrow skill. That changes how you think about where to invest. If capability transfers across domains, then the question becomes less "which subjects do we need to cover" and more "what environments give the clearest reasoning signal." And it also changes how you think about evaluation, because if models are picking up abilities you didn't explicitly train for, you'd better be measuring broadly, including for the capabilities you might not want to show up.

I thought that was a really interesting sign of generalization. You’re training on math, but then you see improvements on GPQA, which asks science questions. That suggests the model might be learning something about how to reason through a problem that carries over beyond the subject it was trained on.

I’d be careful about drawing too strong a conclusion from that result alone. But it raises an exciting question: when we teach a model to reason in one domain, how much of that ability transfers to other domains?

sol-6.1.text:
What I found exciting was that the improvement seemed to transfer beyond the subject the model was trained on. You train on math, where you can check whether an answer is right, and then you see gains on a challenging science benchmark like GPQA. That suggests the model may be learning something more general about how to reason through a problem, rather than just getting better at a particular kind of math question.

I’d be careful about drawing too broad a conclusion from one benchmark, but it was an encouraging early signal: perhaps training reasoning in a domain with clear feedback could help in domains where that feedback is harder to get.
